lessonTitle: IP in Engineering Practice: Searching, Claims and Ownership

blocks.text: A start-up spends 18 months developing a self-tensioning drive-chain mechanism, only to receive a letter from a competitor citing a patent granted six years earlier. A two-hour patent search at the start of the project would have shown the claim and let the team design around it or license it. Engineers who can search patents and read claims avoid both wasted effort and infringement.

blocks.markdown: Patent documents are the largest free technical library in the world. Each one has a **bibliographic page** (title, applicant, dates, classification), an **abstract**, a **description** and, most important legally, the **claims**. The claims define the legal boundary of the monopoly; the description only explains and supports them.

blocks.title: Patent classification
blocks.text: A hierarchical scheme that labels patents by technical subject, independent of the words used. The International Patent Classification (IPC) and the Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) both start with a section letter, such as F for mechanical engineering, followed by class, subclass and group (for example F16H covers gearing).

blocks.markdown: A good basic search combines **classification** and **keywords**. Keywords find documents using your words but miss synonyms (a 'coupling' may be called a 'joint', 'connector' or 'fitting'). Classification finds documents about the same technical subject regardless of vocabulary. Use keywords to discover the right classes, then search the classes to find documents that keywords miss.

headers: Example for a self-adjusting chain tensioner
rows: 1. Define the problem
State function and key features in plain words
Maintain chain tension automatically as the chain wears
2. Choose keywords and synonyms
List alternatives and truncations
chain OR belt OR drive; tension* OR tighten*; automatic* OR self-adjust*
3. Find classes
Use a keyword hit to read its CPC/IPC codes, then search the class
Class for chain or belt tension means within F16H
4. Combine
Use Boolean operators and the classification together
(chain OR belt) AND tension* AND class code
5. Screen
Read abstracts and claims; note dates and family members
Record publication numbers, dates and claim 1
6. Check status
Is it in force, expired, or only a pending application, and in which countries?
Patents are territorial; a UK grant does not cover the US
blocks.caption: A basic patent search workflow.

blocks.title: Building a search string
blocks.prompt: A team is designing a hand-operated pipe clamp that locks onto a pipe by an eccentric cam and wants to know whether similar clamps are already patented. Construct a search strategy.

steps.text: Function in plain words: clamp, pipe, cam-operated locking, quick release.
Keywords with synonyms and truncation: (clamp* OR clip OR collar OR brace) AND (pipe OR tube* OR conduit) AND (cam OR eccentric OR lever).

Classification: run the keyword search in a free database such as Espacenet or Google Patents, look up the CPC codes of the most relevant hits (clamps and hose or pipe clips fall in the F16 section), and re-run with those codes in place of some keywords.
Screen and record: read the claims of the top results, record number, date and legal status, and note family members in other countries.

blocks.answer: The strategy pairs a Boolean keyword string with the classification codes of the nearest hits, then screens by claims and legal status.

blocks.markdown: To read a claim, locate the **independent claims**. They stand alone and do not refer to another claim; **dependent claims** begin 'The device of claim 1, wherein ...' and add features. A claim is a list of **elements**. The infringement test is the *all-elements rule*: a product literally infringes a claim only if it contains every element of that claim. Extra features do not avoid infringement; a missing element does, subject to any rule on equivalents in the jurisdiction, which a lawyer should assess.

blocks.title: Does a design fall within claim 1?
blocks.prompt: Claim 1 of a patent reads: 'A bicycle brake lever comprising: a body; a pivot pin; a lever blade pivotally mounted on the pivot pin; a return spring biasing the blade; and a reach-adjustment screw.' Product A has all five features plus a built-in bell. Product B has the first four but adjusts reach with a rotating cam instead of a screw. Decide for each.

steps.text: Break claim 1 into elements: (1) body, (2) pivot pin, (3) lever blade on the pin, (4) return spring, (5) reach-adjustment screw.
Product A: contains elements 1 to 5, and the bell is an additional feature. By the all-elements rule it falls within claim 1.

Product B: contains elements 1 to 4 but not a screw. It does not literally infringe claim 1 as worded, but whether a cam is an equivalent to a screw is a legal question, so it should be checked with a patent attorney before launch.
Also check whether other independent claims exist and whether the patent is in force in the target country.

blocks.answer: Product A is within claim 1; Product B is outside the literal scope but needs legal advice on equivalence.

blocks.title: Read the claims, not the abstract or the title
blocks.text: The abstract is a summary and has no legal force. Infringement is decided by the wording of the claims, in the countries where the patent is in force and has not expired.

rows: Employee invents in the course of normal duties
Generally belongs to the employer (in the UK, under the Patents Act 1977, section 39)
Disclose to the employer promptly
Employee invents outside duties, using own time and resources
Generally belongs to the employee, but check the contract
Read the employment contract for assignment clauses
Joint project between two companies or a university and a company
Depends on the collaboration agreement; without one, ownership may be shared or disputed
Agree background and foreground IP before work begins
Contractor or consultant
Usually belongs to the contractor unless assigned in writing
Use a written assignment
blocks.caption: IP ownership in typical working arrangements (general principles; local law varies).

blocks.markdown: In collaborations, distinguish **background IP** (what each party brings, which stays with its owner) from **foreground IP** (what is created during the project, whose ownership must be agreed). Good agreements also cover licence rights, publication, confidentiality and what happens if one party leaves.

blocks.title: Agree it in writing before the work starts
blocks.text: Disputes over ownership arise when the agreement is silent or was signed after the invention. Employment contracts and collaboration agreements are where ownership is decided in practice.

points: A basic patent search combines classification codes and keywords with synonyms, then screens by claims and legal status.
Infringement is decided by the claims: a design falls within an independent claim if it contains all of its elements, whatever else it contains.
Ownership of inventions depends on employment terms and collaboration agreements, which should define background and foreground IP before the work begins.

questions.stem: Why should a patent search for a new turbine seal combine classification codes with keywords?

options.text: Keywords are legally required by patent offices
Classification finds documents on the same technical subject even if they use different words for it
Classification codes show who owns the patent
Keywords only search patents that are expired

questions.correctOptionText: Classification finds documents on the same technical subject even if they use different words for it

distractorRationale.b: Correct: documents may call a 'seal' a 'gasket' or 'packing', so classification catches vocabulary differences.
distractorRationale.c: Ownership is in the bibliographic data, not the class code.
distractorRationale.d: Keyword searches cover all documents in the database.

questions.explanation: Different authors use different words for the same device. Classification groups patents by technology, so using it with keywords reduces the risk of missing relevant documents.

questions.stem: A student searching for patents on a magnetic coupling for pump drives uses the string 'magnet coupling'. Which change would most improve it?

options.text: Add synonyms and truncation such as (magnet* OR magnetic) AND (coupl* OR clutch OR drive) AND pump*
Search only for the company name
Remove all keywords
Use only the patent number

questions.correctOptionText: Add synonyms and truncation such as (magnet* OR magnetic) AND (coupl* OR clutch OR drive) AND pump*

distractorRationale.a: Correct: synonyms and truncation increase recall of relevant documents.
distractorRationale.b: A company name does not search the technology.
distractorRationale.d: A number finds a single document only.

questions.explanation: A narrow string misses patents using different wording. Truncation and synonyms combined with Boolean operators broaden the search to cover alternative terms.

questions.stem: A patent has the following claims. Claim 1: 'A hydraulic coupling comprising a male part, a female part and a locking sleeve.' Claim 2: 'The coupling of claim 1, wherein the sleeve is spring-loaded.' Claim 5: 'A method of connecting a hose comprising inserting a male part into a female part.' Which are independent claims?

options.text: Claims 1 and 5
Claim 2 only
Claims 2 and 5
Claim 1 only

distractorRationale.a: Correct: claims 1 and 5 do not refer to another claim; claim 2 depends on claim 1.
distractorRationale.b: Claim 2 refers to claim 1, so it is dependent.
distractorRationale.d: Claim 5 stands alone as a method claim, so it is also independent.

questions.explanation: An independent claim does not refer to another claim, while a dependent claim adds features to one. Claim 5, although a method claim, makes no reference to another claim, so it is independent.

questions.stem: Claim 1 of a patent reads: 'A door latch comprising a housing, a spring-loaded pawl and a striker plate.' A competitor sells a latch with a housing, a spring-loaded pawl, a striker plate and an integral key lock. Does the product fall within claim 1?

options.text: No, because the key lock is not mentioned in the claim
Yes, because it contains every element of claim 1, and the extra key lock does not avoid it
No, because the patent only covers latches without locks
Only if the competitor knew about the patent

questions.correctOptionText: Yes, because it contains every element of claim 1, and the extra key lock does not avoid it

distractorRationale.a: Extra features do not remove a product from the scope of a claim.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: by the all-elements rule, a product with every element of the claim is within it.
distractorRationale.c: The claim contains no such limitation.
distractorRationale.d: Infringement of a granted patent does not generally depend on knowledge.

questions.explanation: A claim is infringed if every element is present. Adding features does not escape the claim. The infringer's knowledge may affect remedies but not whether the product is within the claim.

questions.stem: A mechanical engineer employed to design gearboxes invents an improved bearing arrangement as part of her normal duties during working hours. Under general UK principles (Patents Act 1977, section 39), who normally owns the invention?

options.text: The employer
The engineer alone
The patent office
Whoever files first, regardless of employment

distractorRationale.a: Correct: inventions made in the course of normal duties belong to the employer.
distractorRationale.b: Only if made outside duties and without employer resources, subject to the contract.
distractorRationale.c: The patent office grants rights but does not own inventions.
distractorRationale.d: Filing does not override rightful ownership.

questions.explanation: Under the general rule, an invention made in the course of the employee's normal duties belongs to the employer. Contract terms and the facts of the case matter, and local law differs.

questions.stem: A company and a university sign a collaboration agreement to develop a heat exchanger. The university brings an existing surface-coating process; the company brings a prototype body. What should the agreement specify for IP created during the project?

options.text: Nothing, because the law will assign it to the larger party
Ownership of foreground IP, licence rights to background IP and rules on publication
Only who pays for the prototypes
That no patents may ever be filed

questions.correctOptionText: Ownership of foreground IP, licence rights to background IP and rules on publication

distractorRationale.a: There is no such automatic rule; silence invites disputes.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: agreements distinguish background IP from foreground IP and define ownership, licences and publication.
distractorRationale.c: Costs matter but do not settle IP.
distractorRationale.d: Prohibiting patents defeats a typical purpose of collaboration.

questions.explanation: Ownership of the new IP must be agreed, and background IP remains with its owner but may need licences. Publication and confidentiality terms matter to a university and to a company seeking patent protection.

questions.stem: If two organisations work together and no agreement covers IP, the inventions are automatically owned by whichever party has more employees.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: There is no such rule. Ownership follows from who invented what and the law of the jurisdiction, which is why disputes arise and why an agreement should be concluded before the work begins.

questions.stem: Your team plans to develop a self-adjusting brake pad wear compensator for a bicycle disc brake. Describe how you would carry out a basic patent search before committing to the design, including the choice of keywords, use of classification and how you would screen the results.
markingGuide: Defines function and features in plain words
Lists keywords with synonyms and truncation, combined with Boolean operators
Uses classification (CPC/IPC) found from relevant hits, and searches the class
Uses a free database such as Espacenet or Google Patents
Screens by reading claims, not just titles or abstracts, and notes dates and family members
Checks legal status and territory; records the search for later review
questions.explanation: A complete answer shows the sequence from function to keywords to classification to screening and status. Reading the claims and checking legal status distinguish a professional search from casual browsing.

questions.stem: A patent has independent claim 1: 'A tool holder comprising a shank, a collet having a tapered bore, and a clamping nut engaging a thread on the shank.' A competitor's holder has a shank, a collet with a tapered bore, and a clamping nut engaging a thread on the collet housing, not on the shank. Analyse whether it falls within claim 1 and what further steps the competitor should take.
markingGuide: Breaks the claim into elements (shank, collet with tapered bore, clamping nut engaging a thread on the shank)
Compares each element; the first two are present
Notes the nut engages the housing, not the shank, so a literal element is missing
Concludes there may be no literal infringement but that equivalence may be argued
Recommends legal advice from a patent attorney, checking other independent and dependent claims and legal status
Notes the all-elements rule: extra features do not avoid infringement, a missing one may
questions.explanation: The marker rewards a systematic element-by-element comparison and a cautious conclusion. The answer should not assert non-infringement without recognising the equivalence and other-claims issues.

questions.stem: A graduate engineer is employed by a pump company. Over a weekend, using her own laptop at home, she designs a new impeller shape that is related to the company's products. A second case: two small firms jointly test a valve design without any written agreement. For each case, explain the factors determining ownership of the IP and how the problem could be avoided.
markingGuide: Employment case: ownership depends on whether the invention was made in the course of normal duties and the employment contract's terms
Relatedness to the employer's business and use of company resources or information are relevant
Recommends disclosure to the employer and reading the contract before filing anything
Collaboration case: without an agreement ownership is uncertain, possibly joint, and rights to exploit may be limited
Agreement should define background and foreground IP, ownership, licences, publication and confidentiality
Agreements should be signed before the work starts
questions.explanation: Both cases show that ownership turns on agreements and circumstances rather than on who has the laptop or the larger budget. The practical lesson is to settle the terms in writing early.
